title: Bring On the 'Interrogazione'!
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: Drawing on her own year as a teenage exchange student in Italy, Martinko describes the interrogazione -- a mandatory, high-stakes oral examination in which a teacher questions each student individually at the front of the class -- and proposes reviving something like it in North American schools specifically as a response to AI-enabled cheating. She argues the practice is inherently 'cheat-proof' because it requires real-time, unaided articulation of understanding, while also building self-presentation and confidence-under-pressure skills that written coursework doesn't train. She backs this with the University of Chicago's decision to ban laptops and smartphones across its Social Sciences Collegiate Division, quoting the university's own memo framing the move as protecting students' ability to think and argue without 'the cacophony of other (disembodied and non-human) voices in the room.' The piece frames oral, in-person assessment as a direct structural countermeasure to AI in education, not merely a nostalgic pedagogical preference.
points: Martinko proposes the Italian interrogazione -- a mandatory, unaided oral exam conducted one-on-one at the front of the class -- as a structural, cheat-proof response to AI use in student work.

She cites the University of Chicago's 2026 decision to remove laptops and phones from its Social Sciences Collegiate Division classes, quoting the university's memo on protecting face-to-face, unaided thinking.
The piece argues oral examination trains a distinct skill set -- on-the-spot argument construction and confident self-presentation -- that written, take-home coursework does not.

Martinko frames the proposal explicitly as a tool to 'reverse the cognitive decline we're witnessing in students,' tying it to a broader case against classroom AI dependence rather than presenting it as merely an anti-cheating trick.
quotes: It was there that I discovered the infamous interrogazione, or oral examination, which every Italian high school student knows about (and most of them dread). The interrogazione forms a significant part of every student's grade; the other part comes from written tests and assignments. There's no way out of it.

The idea behind the interrogazione is to develop clear, well-structured arguments and on-the-spot thinking skills. It's an effective way to consolidate knowledge in a student's mind. It forces them to understand a concept when it has to be explained to someone else.
Not only does it cheat-proof the testing, but it also trains those additional spontaneous thinking-and-speaking skills in students, contributing to a better-rounded education overall.
The move is meant to ensure that students can "read, write, and think without dependence on AI.

These guidelines afford students the freedom to think for themselves, to listen to one another without the cacophony of other (disembodied and non-human) voices in the room, to make mistakes, and to change their minds as they engage with thinkers of the past, with us, and with their fellow students in good faith, face-to-face.

And at this point, we need as many tools as we can get to reverse the cognitive decline we're witnessing in students, and maybe it's as simple as having students stand up and talk about what they've learned.
